body.text: A cost-plus contract reimburses a research contractor's allowable labor, supplies, and overhead plus an agreed fee. Under U.S. federal tax law, research performed under standard cost-plus, cost-plus fixed fee, or time-and-materials contracts is funded research, so the performing contractor cannot claim the IRC § 41 R&D tax credit, while the paying client may generally claim 65% as contract research expenses.

Under United States federal income tax law, research and development (R&D) activities executed pursuant to a standard Cost-Plus Contract (CPC), Cost-Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF) contract, or Time-and-Materials (T&M) agreement are statutorily disqualified from the performing contractor's Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41. Because IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) (incorporated for contemporary tax years via Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(9)) exclude any research "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)," a performing contractor may claim Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) only if it satisfies a cumulative two-pronged regulatory test: (1) payment under the agreement must be contingent upon the technical success of the research (the Financial Risk Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1)), and (2) the performing taxpayer must retain substantial rights in the resulting research without paying the client for their use (the Substantial Rights Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3)). Standard Cost-Plus arrangements guarantee reimbursement of allowable direct labor, supplies, and allocable overhead alongside an agreed fee regardless of technical outcome, shifting 100% of the financial risk of research failure to the paying client and rendering the contractor's outlays fully funded.

Narrow exceptions apply where a Cost-Plus framework is structurally modified or strictly segregated from self-funded activities. Specifically, uncompensated costs incurred by a contractor above a binding contractual Not-to-Exceed (NTE) ceiling in a Cost-Plus Guaranteed Maximum Price (CPGMP) agreement—or payments tied strictly to verifiable technical acceptance milestones under a Cost-Plus with Success-Based Fee (SBF) arrangement—may qualify as unfunded QREs under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) and § 1.41-2(e)(2), provided the contractor also retains substantial rights in the resulting intellectual property. However, as established by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), a capped Cost-Plus ceiling does not transfer financial risk to the contractor if monthly progress billings beneath the cap are payable regardless of technical success and the cap remains subject to equitable adjustment for scope changes. Conversely, on the paying client's side, guaranteed Cost-Plus reimbursements paid to a third-party researcher generally qualify as Contract Research Expenses (CREs) subject to the 65% statutory limitation of IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 3, whereas any contingent success bonus is excluded from the client's CREs under Example 4.
Executive Analysis of Cost-Plus Reimbursement in Federal Tax Law
Contractual Mechanics of the Cost-Plus Model in Research and Development

The Cost-Plus Contract (CPC) functions as a foundational commercial instrument in complex research and development (R&D) engagements where technical uncertainty, specialized engineering requirements, and evolving project parameters prevent accurate upfront cost estimation. Under a standard CPC framework, the contracting client (the payer, research recipient, or funder) commits to reimbursing the performing entity (the contractor or research provider) for all allowable direct and allocable indirect expenses incurred during project execution—principally direct engineering labor, raw materials, consumable supplies, and allocable overhead—while paying an additional negotiated fee representing the contractor's profit margin. That additional compensation may be structured either as a predetermined static dollar figure, known under the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and commercial contracting practice as a Cost-Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF), or as a defined percentage markup applied to actual incurred expenditures, alongside incentive-based variants positioned between fixed-price and cost-reimbursement contracts.

Operationally, the Cost-Plus mechanism establishes an open-book accounting relationship between the contracting parties. Because emerging scientific or engineering obstacles frequently invalidate fixed development budgets during early-stage prototyping or experimental design, guaranteeing reimbursement for actual expenditures enables technical teams to pursue iterative experimentation without facing immediate insolvency from unforeseen cost overruns. In aerospace, defense, environmental engineering, and scientific consulting sectors, cost-reimbursement pricing allows project specifications to evolve dynamically as empirical test data is gathered. However, the very commercial attribute that makes a Cost-Plus arrangement attractive to an R&D service provider—complete insulation from project cost volatility and guaranteed recovery of invested working capital—fundamentally alters the federal income tax treatment of those expenditures under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC).
The Statutory Conflict Between Cost Recovery and IRC Section 41

Within U.S. federal income tax law, the use of a Cost-Plus Contract serves as a primary determinant of whether a performing contractor may claim the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41. Enacted originally as part of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 to incentivize American industry to commit additional private capital to technological innovation, the statutory framework of IRC § 41 is designed to subsidize taxpayers that invest their own funds and assume genuine economic jeopardy in the pursuit of technological advancement. Specifically, IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) establishes the "funded research" exclusion, which explicitly disqualifies from the definition of qualified research "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)".

Implementing rules under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)—which remain the controlling regulatory authority for contemporary taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, through explicit incorporation by reference under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(9)—stipulate that research performed under contract for another party is deemed "funded," and thus statutorily excluded from the performing party's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), if the performing taxpayer either bears no financial risk in the event of technical failure or fails to retain substantial rights in the resulting intellectual property (IP). Because a pure Cost-Plus, CPFF, or Time-and-Materials (T&M) contract guarantees the contractor full recovery of incurred expenses alongside a built-in profit margin regardless of whether the research ultimately succeeds or produces a functioning deliverable, the economic risk of technical failure or cost overrun resides entirely with the paying client. From the perspective of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the federal judiciary, permitting a reimbursed contractor to claim the IRC § 41 credit on guaranteed Cost-Plus billings would constitute an impermissible double benefit—collecting guaranteed commercial reimbursement for the expenditure while simultaneously claiming a federal tax subsidy intended to reward financial risk-taking and prevent both parties to a single transaction from claiming duplicate credits on the same underlying research outlays. Consequently, IRS examiners and the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) treat Cost-Plus and T&M compensation clauses as prima facie evidence of disqualified funded research during an IRC § 41 audit.
Taxonomy of Research Contract Structures and Risk Allocation

Determining eligibility for the R&D tax credit requires a granular legal and accounting taxonomy of the underlying compensation mechanism to identify where economic exposure resides at each stage of execution. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) and § 1.41-4A(d), the funded research analysis is applied on an expenditure-by-expenditure and project-by-project basis rather than relying solely on the title of the master agreement. Consequently, even minor structural variations in fee contingencies, acceptance testing preconditions, or reimbursement ceilings can shift the tax classification of underlying wages and supplies from excluded funded activities to eligible QREs.

Agreed percentage markup added to actual incurred costs.
100% borne by the client; 0% borne by the contractor.
Ineligible (Funded Research): Fails the Financial Risk Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1).
Cost-Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF)
100% reimbursement of all allowable project costs incurred.
Predetermined fixed dollar fee that does not fluctuate with actual project costs.
100% borne by the client; guaranteed cost recovery and fixed fee insulate contractor from economic loss.
Ineligible (Funded Research): Guaranteed cost recovery and fixed fee negate economic risk for the contractor (client may claim 65% of total paid under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(5) Ex. 3).
Time-and-Materials (T&M)
Direct reimbursement for labor hours at specified billing rates plus actual material costs.
Profit embedded within hourly labor billing rates and material handling markups.
100% borne by the client across all billed hours and materials unless payment is expressly conditioned on technical acceptance.
Ineligible (Funded Research): Treated identically to pure Cost-Plus during IRS examinations when billed monthly regardless of success.
Capped Cost-Plus / Guaranteed Maximum Price (CPGMP / NTE)
Reimbursement of labor and expenses plus markup only up to a contractual Not-to-Exceed (NTE) ceiling.
Markup paid only within the NTE ceiling; eroded or eliminated if costs exceed the cap.
Mixed / Bifurcated: Client bears risk up to the NTE cap; contractor absorbs 100% of excess costs above an immovable cap.

Partially / Conditionally Eligible: Reimbursed costs up to the cap are funded and excluded (Geosyntec, 776 F.3d 1330); uncompensated costs incurred above a fixed funding cap may qualify under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) if Substantial Rights are retained.
Cost-Plus with Success-Based Fees (SBF)
Base cost structure modified by performance-contingent payment, milestone acceptance, or clawback provisions.
Substantial portion of fee or cost recoupment contingent on verifiable technical milestones.
Shared risk depending on whether non-payment or refund clauses apply upon technical failure.

Conditionally Eligible: Qualifies only to the extent payment is genuinely contingent on technical success (paid for the result rather than performance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) & Ex. 4) and Substantial Rights are retained.
Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP)
Predetermined lump-sum or milestone price paid only upon successful delivery and acceptance of conforming output.
Residual margin between fixed contract price and actual costs incurred.
100% borne by the contractor for both cost overruns and technical non-acceptance.
Eligible: Satisfies the Financial Risk Test for 100% of qualifying expenses when payment is contingent on technical success, subject to the Substantial Rights Test.

body.text: Standard Cost-Plus, Time-and-Materials, and Cost-Plus Fixed Fee Arrangements

Standard Cost-Plus and Time-and-Materials (T&M) agreements transfer 100% of project cost volatility to the customer. Because the contractor invoices the client periodically—typically monthly—for every hour of engineering labor expended and every unit of test material or supply consumed, the contractor's general ledger reflects a dollar-for-dollar reimbursement (plus markup) that extinguishes any net economic outlay. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), because the contractor is entitled to payment for all work performed during the billing period regardless of whether the research succeeds, any risk of nonpayment (such as administrative invoice disputes over missing paperwork) is unrelated to the technical outcome of the research, rendering the entire arrangement funded.

The Cost-Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF) variant refines this pricing model by decoupling the profit fee from total expenditure volume so the contractor has minimal responsibility for performance costs and no financial incentive to inflate project expenditures. In a CPFF contract, the performing entity is reimbursed for 100% of all allowable incurred costs and receives a static, predetermined dollar fee that remains unchanged regardless of how high actual costs climb. While CPFF contracts are widely deployed in government and commercial R&D when initial cost projections are highly uncertain, the presence of guaranteed cost recovery alongside a fixed profit margin reinforces the IRS audit position under both IRC § 41 (Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 3) and IRC § 174 (IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 6.05 Example) that the contractor faces neither the risk of out-of-pocket operating loss nor the risk of uncompensated performance failure.
Capped Cost-Plus and Guaranteed Maximum Price Structures

A critical legal and accounting divergence occurs when contracting parties execute a Capped Cost-Plus agreement, formally designated in commercial and engineering practice as a Cost-Plus Guaranteed Maximum Price (CPGMP) contract or a Cost-Plus contract subject to a "Not-to-Exceed" (NTE) ceiling. Under a CPGMP structure, the client reimburses the contractor for direct labor, materials, and an agreed percentage or fixed markup, but strictly up to a contractually fixed maximum dollar ceiling. Once cumulative project expenditures reach an immovable NTE ceiling, the client's reimbursement obligation terminates; if technical completion requires additional engineering hours, redesigns, or test materials beyond that cap, the performing contractor must absorb 100% of the excess expenditure out of its own capital.

This contractual ceiling creates a bifurcated risk profile that requires careful analysis under both Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3) and federal appellate case law. Below the NTE cap, where the contractor bills monthly for time and materials without conditioning payment on technical acceptance of a successful research result, the arrangement operates as a standard funded Cost-Plus contract, and all reimbursed expenditures up to the cap are disqualified. As the Eleventh Circuit held in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), the mere presence of a maximum price ceiling does not convert reimbursed progress billings beneath the cap into unfunded research, particularly where payment is not contingent on achieving a successful technical result and where the ceiling can be adjusted through change orders or addenda. Above an immovable NTE cap, however, where the contractor absorbs actual qualified research expenditures in excess of the total funding entitlement, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) provides that if the performing taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research, the research is treated as funded only "to the extent of the payments (and fair market value of any property) to which the taxpayer becomes entitled by performing the research". Thus, uncompensated qualified expenditures incurred in excess of the guaranteed maximum funding ceiling—when paired with retained substantial IP rights—constitute the primary structural pathway for claiming excess QREs within a Capped Cost-Plus framework.

Conversely, from the paying client's perspective under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 3, if the contract was entered into prior to performance, performed on the client's behalf, and required the client to bear the full $165,000 expense regardless of success, the client may claim 65% of the $165,000 payment ($107,250) as a Contract Research Expense (CRE).

When actual qualified research expenditures reach $150,000, the first $100,000 is reimbursed by the client and is disqualified as funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i). If the project also included nonqualified expenses alongside qualified expenses, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) requires that 100% of the $100,000 funding be allocated directly against otherwise qualified research expenses unless the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the IRS the total amount of research expenses, that total research expenses exceed the funding, and that otherwise qualified research expenses exceed 65% of the funding (with at least 65% of the funding applied against otherwise qualified research expenses in all events).

In Hypothetical Scenario C, involving a Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) lump sum of $100,000, the contractor agrees to deliver a functioning technical prototype for a fixed price of $100,000 strictly contingent upon client acceptance. During execution, the contractor incurs $150,000 in actual in-house wages and supplies, absorbing a $50,000 operating loss. Crucially, because the entire $150,000 expenditure was placed at risk of non-recovery if the technical milestone failed acceptance, 100% of the $150,000 in-house expenditure ($150,000 of QREs) satisfies the Financial Risk Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), qualifying in full for the contractor if it also retains substantial rights. Conversely, on the paying client's side, if a client pays a fixed $100,000 sum under a research contract where the client bears the expense regardless of success (as in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 1) and the contractor retains no substantial rights, the client's eligible Contract Research Expense (CRE) is statutorily restricted to 65% of the amount paid under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A):

However, if the client's $100,000 payment is strictly contingent on the success of the research, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) deems the client's payment to be for the purchase of a finished "product or result rather than the performance of the research," disqualifying the client from claiming any CRE ($0), and if the contractor simultaneously failed to retain substantial rights, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) dictates that neither the client nor the contractor may claim any portion of the expenditures as QREs.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Funded Research Exclusion
Qualified Research Expenses and the 65 Percent Contract Research Limitation

Under IRC § 41(a) and § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer may claim a tax credit based on Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. The statute divides QREs into two exclusive categories: (1) in-house research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2) (comprising taxable W-2 wages as defined in IRC § 3401(a) paid to employees for engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(B), non-depreciable tangible supplies consumed in qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(C), and amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research), and (2) Contract Research Expenses (CREs) under IRC § 41(b)(3). When a taxpayer engages a third party (other than an employee of the taxpayer) to perform qualified research on its behalf, IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1) mandate that only 65% of the amount paid or incurred to the contractor may be included as a CRE. Furthermore, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(4), any prepaid contract research expense attributable to qualified research conducted after the close of the taxable year can only be taken into account in the taxable year in which the qualified research is actually conducted.

The policy objective linking the 65% CRE limitation and the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) is to ensure that the tax incentive accrues exclusively to the entity that commits capital at risk while preventing double-claiming by both parties to a research contract. Courts refer to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) as "mirror image rules" designed to ensure that the contractor and client do not both claim a research credit on the same work. When a service provider works under a Cost-Plus contract, tax law recognizes that the client—not the contractor—is funding the activity. Furthermore, the 35% statutory reduction applied to the client's CREs under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) reflects the fact that a contractor's invoice price (such as a Cost-Plus billing) embeds non-qualifying overhead, equipment depreciation, and profit markups alongside direct research wages and supplies—as illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 3, where a client's $300x Cost-Plus payment covering $90x labor, $20x supplies, $50x depreciation on equipment, $40x overhead ($200x total expenses), and a $100x fixed fee yields $195x (65% of $300x) in client CREs.

This risk-and-rights allocation principle aligns with broader federal income tax provisions governing research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC § 174 and IRC § 174A, as addressed in IRS Notice 2023-63 (released September 8, 2023) and modified by IRS Notice 2024-12. Following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206(a)), IRC § 174 required mandatory capitalization and 5-year (60-month domestic) or 15-year (180-month foreign) amortization for Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. In Section 6 of Notice 2023-63, Treasury and the IRS established that a contract research provider's costs are treated as SRE expenditures subject to § 174 only if the provider either bears financial risk under the terms of the contract or has a right to use any resulting "SRE product" in its trade or business or otherwise exploit it through sale, lease, or license. Specifically, in Section 6.05 Example of Notice 2023-63, where Company C engages contractor Company D under a Cost-Plus Fixed-Fee contract ($125,000 actual expenditures reimbursed plus a $25,000 fixed sum, totaling $150,000) with no performance guarantees and no right for Company D to use or exploit any resulting SRE product, the IRS confirmed that Company D may not treat its $125,000 of expenditures as SRE expenditures under § 174, whereas Company C treats the $150,000 paid as an SRE expenditure under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(10) and (b)(3). Subsequently, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302, enacted July 4, 2025) added IRC § 174A (implemented via Revenue Procedure 2025-28), which restored immediate deductibility (or elective amortization over not less than 60 months under § 174A(c)) for domestic R&E expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while retaining 15-year capitalization under IRC § 174 for foreign research (where Revenue Procedure 2025-23, § 7.03(1)(a), as modified by Revenue Procedure 2026-32, § 3.04, continues to permit reliance on Section 6 of Notice 2023-63). Across IRC § 41, § 174, and § 174A, if an expenditure is classified as funded in the hands of the performing contractor under a Cost-Plus contract, it is 100% excluded from the contractor's QREs.
Controlling Mandate of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d)

IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) states that qualified research does not include "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) (applicable to contemporary tax years via Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(9)) establishes the controlling administrative rules for applying this exclusion. Notably, the U.S. Tax Court has rejected post-Loper Bright challenges to the validity of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), reaffirming that its two-part test based on contingent payments and substantial rights remains valid. When evaluating whether and to what extent research is funded, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) mandates that the IRS does not examine the primary statement of work in isolation; rather, "All agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons shall be considered in determining the extent to which the research is funded". Note, however, that for transactions between members of a controlled group of corporations or commonly controlled trades or businesses under IRC § 41(f), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-6(i) treats the group as a single taxpayer, directing that a member performing research for another member includes its in-house research expenses in its own QREs and does not treat intra-group payments as funding the research or as contract research expenses.

Furthermore, for unrelated contracting parties, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(5) (Funding determinable only in subsequent taxable year) imposes a strict procedural presumption against the taxpayer when funding arrangements are contingent, hybrid, or indeterminate at year-end. If, at the time the performing taxpayer files its federal income tax return for a taxable year, it is impossible to determine the exact extent to which particular research performed during that year may be funded by another party—for example, where a CPGMP contract has not yet breached its Not-to-Exceed ceiling or where contingent milestone adjustments remain open—the regulation mandates that "the taxpayer shall treat the research as completely funded for purposes of completing that return". Only when the amount of funding is finally determined in a subsequent taxable year should the taxpayer amend that return (and any interim returns) to reflect the proper amount of funding. This rule places a substantial contemporaneous burden on contractors operating under hybrid Cost-Plus agreements to establish non-funded status before claiming credits on an original return.
The Two-Pronged Eligibility Test: Financial Risk and Substantial Rights

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), a contractor performing research for an unrelated client can escape the funded research exclusion only by satisfying a cumulative two-pronged regulatory gate. Failing either prong renders the research funded and disqualifies the expenditure under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).

The first gate is Prong I, the Financial Risk Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), under which research is treated as funded unless amounts payable under the agreement are "contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2))". For a contractor to bear genuine financial risk under Prong I, the contract must compel the contractor to bear the research costs upon failure—requiring the contractor to forfeit billing, incur uncompensated expenses to correct rejected work, or refund advanced payments if the research fails to produce the desired product or result. Standard Cost-Plus, CPFF, and T&M contracts automatically fail at Prong I because they guarantee reimbursement of incurred costs (and a fixed or percentage profit margin) for the performance of work regardless of technical failure, routing those expenditures directly into the funded research exclusion. By contrast, Capped Cost-Plus (CPGMP) agreements bifurcate at an immovable Not-to-Exceed ceiling: reimbursed expenditures up to the cap fail Prong I and are disqualified (Geosyntec, 776 F.3d 1330), whereas uncompensated over-cap losses absorbed by the contractor under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)—alongside qualifying Firm-Fixed-Price contracts, contingent Success-Based Fee structures under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 4, and self-funded pre-award Internal R&D—satisfy Prong I and advance to the second regulatory gate. Overcoming Prong I within a contracted structure requires enforceable risk-shifting clauses, such as defined acceptance criteria tied to measurable technical performance results, non-payment or rejection provisions triggered by failure to meet contract specifications, or rigorous quality-assurance obligations that subject cost recovery to material economic hazard.

The second gate is Prong II, the Substantial Rights Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and § 1.41-4A(d)(3) (in conjunction with Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i)–(ii)), which dictates that even where a contractor bears full financial risk under a Firm-Fixed-Price or over-cap CPGMP arrangement, the expenditure is still treated as fully funded if the performing taxpayer "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research". As clarified by the Federal Circuit in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), retaining substantial rights does not require the contractor to hold exclusive rights to exclude others, but the contractor must retain the right to use the research results in its trade or business without paying the client for that right. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and § 1.41-4A(d)(3), if an agreement confers on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research, requires the taxpayer to pay for the right to use the results, or requires the contractor to obtain customer permission before using any results, data, documents, or technical concepts developed during the project, the contractor does not retain substantial rights. Moreover, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly states that "[i]ncidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Similarly, for IRC § 174 purposes under IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 6.02(4) and 6.04, a research provider holds an SRE product right only if it has a right to use a resulting pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, computer software, or similar property (subject to protection under applicable domestic or foreign law) in its trade or business or otherwise exploit it through sale, lease, or license without obtaining an unrelated party's approval, whereas mere know-how gained through the performance of research services that is not subject to protection under domestic or foreign law does not give rise to an SRE product. Because commercial buyers of Cost-Plus R&D services routinely demand both open-book cost reimbursement and exclusive IP assignment, typical Cost-Plus engagements fail both Prong I and Prong II simultaneously.
Judicial Precedent Governing Cost-Reimbursement Disqualification

Federal appellate and trial courts evaluating R&D tax credit refund suits have consistently upheld the Treasury Department's regulatory interpretation that cost-reimbursement contracts strip the performing contractor of the financial risk required by IRC § 41.
Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States and the Concession on Pure Cost-Plus Contracts

The litigation in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, No. 9:12-cv-80334, 2013 WL 5328479 (S.D. Fla. Apr. 17, 2013), aff'd, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), alongside the Court of Federal Claims decision in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), serves as the benchmark judicial precedent addressing the tax treatment of Cost-Plus and Capped Cost-Plus arrangements. Geosyntec, a specialized consulting and engineering firm working on environmental, natural resources, and geological infrastructure projects, filed suit seeking a $1,677,432 federal income tax refund under IRC § 41 for research expenses incurred across hundreds of client contracts during tax years 2002, 2003, 2004, and 2005. As reflected in the baseline record and parallel litigation in Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 512), standard uncapped Cost-Plus contracts—where the paying client assumes the entire economic risk for all time and material costs incurred—do not qualify for the IRC § 41 credit and are eliminated from the scope of eligible research claims.

In Geosyntec, the parties designated six representative contracts for summary judgment review by the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida: three fixed-price contracts and three cost-plus contracts subject to a maximum ceiling (referred to as "capped contracts"). On April 17, 2013, the district court ruled that the three fixed-price contracts were unfunded—leading to a settlement in which Geosyntec received a $255,575 tax refund plus interest for its fixed-price projects—but held that the three capped cost-plus contracts were funded by the clients and therefore ineligible for the credit. Geosyntec appealed the capped cost-plus ruling to the Eleventh Circuit with respect to two agreements—the Cherry Island Contract and the Waste Management (WM) Contract—under which Geosyntec was reimbursed monthly for actual labor and expenses plus a markup, subject to an agreed maximum price cap.

Before the Eleventh Circuit, Geosyntec argued that its capped cost-plus contracts placed it at financial risk because its total compensation was subject to a ceiling, exposing it to the risk of exceeding its budget or failing to earn a profit. In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), the Eleventh Circuit rejected this argument and affirmed summary judgment against Geosyntec, establishing two key principles governing capped Cost-Plus contracts. First, the court held that general "cost-of-performance" or budget overrun risk is not the financial risk with which IRC § 41 is concerned because "the only issue is whether payment was contingent on the success of the research—that is, the financial risk of failure". Second, examining the terms of the Cherry Island and WM contracts, the court found that Geosyntec was entitled to payment each month for all work performed during the previous calendar month regardless of the outcome of its research, that the contracts lacked quality assurance or inspection acceptance preconditions akin to Fairchild, and that the ceiling prices were not immovable because Geosyntec could claim additional compensation via change orders or written addenda for scope changes or unreasonable regulatory demands. Thus, Geosyntec establishes that a Capped Cost-Plus contract remains funded below its cap when periodic cost-reimbursement billings are not contingent on the success of the research.
Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States and Economic Loss Exposure

The principles applied in Geosyntec build directly upon the foundational government contracting precedent established by the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), modified (Feb. 23, 1996). In Fairchild, an aerospace manufacturer entered into a fixed-price incentive contract with the U.S. Air Force to design and produce a training aircraft prototype. Although the Air Force disbursed bi-monthly refundable advance progress payments calculated as a percentage of Fairchild's actual incurred expenditures, the contract incorporated strict quality assurance procedures under which the Air Force evaluated Fairchild's work item-by-item prior to acceptance. Unless and until Fairchild fully succeeded in each phase of the project and delivered results meeting the contract's specifications, it had no right to retain payment; if the Air Force deemed delivered work unacceptable, it could reject the work, require Fairchild to correct the work at its own expense, or accept the work at a reduced price, obligating Fairchild to reimburse the Air Force for unliquidated advances in the event of failure.

Reversing the Court of Federal Claims, the Federal Circuit held that whether payment is contingent upon success turns on "who bears the research costs upon failure, not on whether the researcher is likely to succeed in performing the project". Crucially, judicial precedent following Fairchild—including Geosyntec, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 23-1523 (8th Cir. 2024)—distinguishes between true economic loss exposure from research failure (where the contractor's invested wages and supply expenditures remain unrecovered or must be refunded if the work fails technical specifications) and general economic or operational risk. In a standard Cost-Plus or CPFF arrangement, because the contractor is assured full recovery of allowable costs plus a fixed profit fee regardless of technical success, the contractor never faces out-of-pocket loss on its research outlays. Where a contract shields the performer from financial uncertainty and guarantees cost recoupment irrespective of technical outcome, the expenditures are legally funded and ineligible for the credit.
Substantiation Standards, Internal Research Carve-Outs, and IRS Examination Defense

Navigating an IRS examination under the IRC § 41 Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) and the Aerospace Industry Research Credit ATG requires contemporaneous legal and accounting substantiation proving that claimed research expenses were neither directly nor indirectly reimbursed under a client contract.
Pre-Award Internal Research and Development Carve-Outs

Even when a contractor predominantly executes client engagements on a Cost-Plus basis, foundational research conducted internally by the contractor outside the scope of a client reimbursement agreement may remain eligible as self-funded In-House Research Expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2). Specifically, pre-award research, independent foundational scientific investigations, or technical feasibility studies initiated prior to the execution of a definitive client funding contract are typically borne at the contractor's sole financial risk. Furthermore, in the government contracting context, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(4) (Independent research and development under the Federal Acquisition Regulations System and similar provisions) explicitly provides that although the FAR and similar regulations relating to government contracts (fixed-price, cost-plus, etc.) provide for the allocation of certain "independent research and development costs" (IR&D) and "bid and proposal costs" (B&P) of a contractor to contracts entered into with that contractor, any such IR&D and B&P costs paid to a taxpayer by reason of such a contract "shall not be treated as funding the underlying research activities except to the extent the 'independent research and development costs' and 'bid and proposal costs' are properly" allocable to long-term contracts under IRC § 451 / § 460.

To prevent IRS examiners from sweeping pre-award Internal R&D (IR&D) into a subsequent Cost-Plus contract under the "all agreements" rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), the contractor must establish a strict chronological and accounting firewall. The performing entity must substantiate that the IR&D project was authorized, initiated, and funded internally prior to—and independent of—any guaranteed client reimbursement commitment. This requires contemporaneous internal Authorization for Expenditure (AFE) requests, distinct internal project charge codes, employee time-tracking logs, and technical meeting minutes demonstrating that the expenditures were paid or incurred in carrying on the contractor's own trade or business before the client CPC took effect.
The Three-Part Regulatory Test for Contract Research Expenses

Where a paying client seeks to claim third-party Cost-Plus payments as Contract Research Expenses (CREs) under IRC § 41(b)(3)—or where IRS examiners evaluate the reciprocal "mirror image" rights between payer and performer—the contractual arrangement is measured against the mandatory three-part regulatory test of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) and § 1.41-2(e)(3). Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research only to the extent that it is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that satisfies three cumulative requirements:

items: Prior Agreement Requirement (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)): The research agreement must be entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research (paperwork drawn up at year-end after the research is already finished fails this requirement).

"On Behalf Of" / Entitlement to Results Requirement (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) & (e)(3)): The agreement must explicitly provide that the research be performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, which Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(3) defines as the taxpayer having a right to the research results (though exclusive rights to the results are not required).

Economic Risk / Expense Bearing Requirement (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)): The agreement must require the paying taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) states, if an expense is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement under which payment is contingent on the success of the research, the expense is considered paid for the product or result rather than the performance of the research, and that contingent payment is not a contract research expense.

body.text: In a typical Cost-Plus Fixed-Fee contract (as illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 3), where the client is unconditionally obligated to reimburse the contractor for all expenses ($200x) plus pay a fixed fee ($100x) regardless of technical success and the client retains the rights to the resulting IP, the paying client satisfies all three elements of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) and may claim 65% of the $300x payment ($195x) as a CRE. Conversely, that exact same allocation of risk and IP ownership seals the total exclusion of the expenses for the performing contractor under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and (d)(2). Where a Cost-Plus contract requires the client to reimburse all actual expenses ($200x) and pay an additional $100x bonus only if the research is successful (as in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 4), the contingent $100x bonus is excluded from the client's CREs under paragraph (e)(2), limiting the client's CRE to 65% of the guaranteed $200x cost reimbursement ($130x). Finally, where a contract calls for services other than qualified research or qualified support services (such as outside accounting to keep books and records in Example 7, or bundled project administration, training, or installation), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1) limits the client's 65% CRE computation strictly to the portion of the amount paid or incurred that is attributable to qualified research or qualified services.
Audit Techniques Guide Documentation Checklist

During an IRC § 41 audit, IRS examiners follow the Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) to look past summary general ledger totals and request complete copies of all contracts (including modifications), agreements, letters of understanding, project sub-ledgers, and IP schedules that govern cost recovery.

cells: Master Service Agreements (MSAs), SOWs & Modifications
Funding Status & Financial Risk Allocation

Complete copies of all contracts, modifications, letters of understanding, and Statements of Work showing explicit compensation structures (CPFF, T&M, CPGMP, FFP), milestone payment schedules, non-payment or clawback clauses upon technical failure, and quality assurance / inspection acceptance terms.
Establishes cost recovery mechanics under the "all agreements" rule and proves whether payment is contingent on technical success under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and § 1.41-2(e)(2).
General Ledger, Chart of Accounts & Project Sub-Ledgers
Cost Tracing, Segregation & Cap Monitoring

Granular isolation of risk-bearing costs (Fixed-Price project costs and uncompensated CPGMP costs exceeding an immovable NTE ceiling) from reimbursed Cost-Plus billings, backed by invoices, purchase orders, receipts, W-2 wage records, and work orders.

Required to substantiate exact cost reduction and pro rata allocation when research is partially funded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(ii) or subject to the filing-date rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(5).
Internal Project Authorization Requests (AFEs)
Contemporaneous Self-Funding of Pre-Award IR&D

Dated internal project approvals, distinct IR&D/B&P charge codes, employee time-tracking records, and engineering minutes proving that IR&D was initiated and funded internally prior to the execution of a client CPC.

Substantiates that pre-award expenses were paid or incurred in the taxpayer's own trade or business under IRC § 41(b)(2) and protected from indirect overhead disqualification under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(4).
Intellectual Property Assignments & License Schedules
Substantial Rights Retention

Executed contract clauses proving that the performing taxpayer retains an unfettered right (such as a non-exclusive, perpetual, royalty-free license without needing client permission or paying fees) to use or exploit the research results in its trade or business.

Demonstrates satisfaction of Prong II (Substantial Rights Test) of the funded research exclusion under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3) and Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000).

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Contract Restructuring Protocol

For engineering, architecture, defense, software, and scientific service providers operating in commercial environments that favor cost-reimbursement pricing, preserving eligibility for the IRC § 41 R&D tax credit requires deliberate coordination between legal contracting, cost accounting, and tax compliance teams. While transitioning entirely from Cost-Plus to Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) contracts conditioned on formal technical acceptance provides the clearest legal defense under the Financial Risk Test of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and Fairchild Industries, commercial constraints often necessitate hybrid structures and targeted contractual carve-outs.
Immediate Audit Risk Assessment and Cost Accounting Segregation

The foundational phase of an institutional compliance protocol begins with a comprehensive contract portfolio triage. Legal and tax teams should conduct a systematic review of all active and open-statute historical R&D service agreements (including all contract modifications, addenda, and letters of understanding), segmenting every engagement by compensation mechanism across Pure Cost-Plus, CPFF, T&M, CPGMP/NTE, Cost-Plus with Success-Based Fees, and FFP categories. All pure Cost-Plus, CPFF, and unconditional T&M billings must be excluded from the contractor's QRE base. Immediate analytical priority should then be directed toward hybrid Capped Cost-Plus (CPGMP) agreements to determine: (1) whether actual direct labor and supply expenditures exceeded an immovable NTE ceiling in specific tax years, thereby generating uncompensated excess expenditures under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), and (2) whether any contracts with indeterminate year-end funding must initially be treated as 100% funded on the original return and claimed via an amended return once final funding is resolved under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(5).

Concurrently, organizations must upgrade their job-cost accounting systems to enforce strict project-level and expenditure-level segregation that prevents the commingling of funded and unfunded activities. The general ledger and project accounting architecture should track Fixed-Price contracts in separate cost centers from Cost-Plus contracts, automatically bifurcate CPGMP project costs at the exact dollar threshold of an immovable NTE ceiling (recording excess qualified expenditures as non-reimbursable operating losses while verifying whether the 65% pro rata allocation threshold of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) is met), and isolate pre-award IR&D and FAR-governed indirect IR&D/B&P costs under dedicated AFE charge codes pursuant to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(4).
Contract Drafting Protocols for Risk and Substantial Rights

To protect future R&D claims, legal and contracting departments should establish formal drafting protocols that embed material financial risk of technical failure into R&D service agreements whenever a pure Firm-Fixed-Price structure is commercially unfeasible. As Geosyntec (776 F.3d 1330) demonstrated, merely inserting a maximum price cap into a monthly T&M or Cost-Plus billing structure is insufficient if the contractor is paid for hours worked regardless of technical outcome. Instead, contracts should incorporate either binding Not-to-Exceed ceilings (CPGMP) or Success-Based Fees (SBF) and refundable progress-payment structures modeled on Fairchild Industries (71 F.3d 868) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 4, where cost recoupment and fee retention are explicitly conditioned upon achieving verifiable technical performance milestones and passing rigorous client inspection and acceptance testing.

In parallel, corporate Master Service Agreement templates must be standardized to preserve substantial intellectual property rights for the performing contractor under Prong II. Even where the paying client requires ownership of project-specific deliverables, the contract should explicitly reserve a non-exclusive, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free right and license for the performing contractor to use, adapt, and exploit the underlying research results, know-how, and technical developments in its general trade or business without paying royalties or seeking prior customer permission—thereby satisfying Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3) and the Federal Circuit's standard in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000).
Legal Opinions on Hybrid Structures and Regulatory Advocacy

Because hybrid Capped Cost-Plus agreements and contingent fee arrangements attract heightened IRS examination scrutiny regarding whether and when financial risk genuinely shifted to the contractor, organizations claiming substantial over-cap or milestone-contingent QREs should engage specialized tax counsel to issue a formal legal opinion prior to filing. That opinion should analyze the precise allocation of risk under the NTE and acceptance clauses across all related agreements under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), evaluate any partial funding reductions and pro rata allocations under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(ii), verify compliance with the filing-date certainty mandate of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(5), reconcile the treatment of contract costs with IRC § 174 and § 174A under IRS Notice 2023-63 Section 6 and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and document the legal rationale for the unfunded cost allocation to establish a contemporaneous defense against audit challenges. Finally, industry groups and R&D contractors should participate in proactive regulatory advocacy urging the Treasury Department and the IRS—as they issue proposed and final regulations following Notice 2023-63, Notice 2024-12, and IRC § 174A—to establish clarifying administrative safe harbors that define de minimis contractual risk thresholds or specify which commercial warranty and acceptance clauses suffice to establish financial risk without triggering automatic disqualification under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
